title: Prompting & Spec-Writing
tagline: Turn a vague ask into a structured prompt an AI tool can actually execute against.
intro: A PRD written for a human engineer assumes a lot of shared context — team conventions, prior conversations, 'you know what I mean.' A prompt written for an AI tool can't assume any of that. The skill isn't writing longer specs, it's writing specs that don't rely on anything the reader hasn't been told.

diagram.caption: The five parts of a structured prompt, in order. Each row below builds one part of this template for the I-9 Completion Assistant.

scenario.context: A stakeholder has asked, in Slack: 'Can we use AI to make I-9 review easier for the Meridian Logistics HR team?' That's the entire brief you were given. (The same vague-ask problem shows up constantly across Employer Services — 'can AI help with offboarding paperwork' is the exact same shape of ask, just on a different product line.)
scenario.brief: Your job is to turn that one-line ask into a structured prompt you could actually run against an AI tool — either to draft a first-pass PRD section, or to have the AI draft sample I-9 Completion Assistant flags for you to evaluate. Assume the AI has no memory of anything except what you put in the prompt.

sections.heading: Role
sections.learning: Who should the AI act as? Be specific — 'an I-9 compliance assistant for a logistics employer' beats 'a helpful assistant.' The role sets the vocabulary and judgment the rest of the prompt can lean on.

example.text: You are an I-9 employment-eligibility compliance assistant supporting HR administrators at Meridian Logistics, a trucking and logistics employer using the I-9 product within Equifax Workforce Solutions' Onboarding category.

sections.pitfall: Writing 'You are a helpful assistant' and moving on. A vague role gives the model no vocabulary or judgment to lean on — it defaults to generic customer-service phrasing instead of I-9-specific precision, like citing 'Section 2' correctly instead of guessing at what that means.

field.label: Your turn: Role
field.help: Who should the AI act as for the I-9 Completion Assistant prompt?
field.placeholder: e.g. You are an I-9 compliance assistant for...

sections.heading: Context
sections.learning: State the full situation. What does the AI need to know that a human teammate would already have picked up from context? Nothing implied, nothing assumed.

example.text: Federal law requires Section 1 of Form I-9 completed by the employee's first day, and Section 2 completed by the employer within 3 business days of that date — verified against either one List A document (which proves identity and work authorization together, like a U.S. passport) or one List B document plus one List C document (identity and work authorization proven separately, like a driver's license plus a Social Security card). A new hire has submitted a completed I-9 and photos of their supporting documents.

sections.pitfall: Assuming the AI knows what you know. It doesn't know that List A and List B-plus-List-C are alternatives, not both required, or that asking for List B/C after List A was already presented is itself a compliance problem — unless the prompt says so explicitly, every time.

field.label: Your turn: Context
field.help: State the full situation the AI needs, with nothing implied.
field.placeholder: Include the relevant compliance rule and what's been submitted.

sections.heading: Task
sections.learning: State the instruction, not a question. What exact thing should it produce?

example.text: Compare the submitted I-9 fields and document images against federal I-9 requirements. List every field that is missing, inconsistent, or backed by an expired document, and state which specific requirement each issue violates.

sections.pitfall: Phrasing the task as a question — 'can you check this?' — instead of an instruction. Questions invite a conversational answer; instructions produce a structured one you can actually reuse across every new hire.

field.label: Your turn: Task
field.help: State the instruction as a command, not a question.
field.placeholder: e.g. Compare X against Y and list...

sections.heading: Constraints
sections.learning: What must it never do? What's out of scope? Vague asks fail quietly — a vague prompt won't error out, it'll just produce a plausible-sounding, low-value answer that takes real time to notice is off-target. Constraints are what prevent that.

example.text: Never state that a document is valid or invalid — only that it matches or doesn't match federal requirements as described. Never contact the new hire directly; output is for HR admin review only. If a document type isn't recognized, flag for manual review rather than guessing.

sections.pitfall: Only writing constraints for what could go wrong technically, and skipping the compliance ones. 'Never state a document is valid or invalid' is a constraint you'd only think to write if you already know the AI shouldn't be the one making that legal determination — this is where I-9 knowledge and prompt-writing have to work together.

field.label: Your turn: Constraints
field.help: What must the AI never do, or what's explicitly out of scope?

sections.heading: Output format
sections.learning: What should the result look like, structurally? A good prompt is a reusable artifact — save it, refine it, hand it to a teammate. If you find yourself rewriting the same context every time, that's a sign the prompt should become a template, which is exactly what this exercise produces.

example.text: A bulleted list of issues found, each with: the I-9 field or document affected, the specific requirement it fails to meet, and a suggested next step for the HR admin (e.g., 'request updated document,' 'confirm with employee').

sections.pitfall: Leaving the format loose because 'the AI will figure out something reasonable.' It will — a different reasonable format every time, which makes 40 new hires' worth of output impossible to scan or compare at a glance.

field.label: Your turn: Output format
field.help: What should the result look like structurally?
field.placeholder: Describe the exact shape of the output.
